Un an après le 7 octobre : cinq personne: One Year After October 7: Five People Share Their Experiences of Loss and Suffering
La Converse s’est entretenue avec cinq p: La Converse spoke with five people to show the profound changes that have taken place since October 7, 2023.
Yonatan Zeigen, Raquel Look, Hamza Banar: Yonatan Zeigen, Raquel Look, Hamza Banar, Mohammed R. Mhawish and Yipeng Ge told us about the profound changes in their lives over the past year.
Chaque reportage politique portant sur l: Every political story on the Middle East that I have written over the past 20 years has involved considerations of language, context and sources. The guiding principle behind my editorial decisions has always been the answers to these questions: Which voice or point of view has been left out of the news? How can I centre the experience of those who are hardest hit?
Cette fois-ci, mon objectif était différ: This time, my goal was different. October 7, 2023, like every day since, has become synonymous with immense grief in a range of communities. For many of us, that pain is reinforced daily by horrific images and virulent online comments that only deepen the polarization of society today.
Je crois que faire preuve de compassion: I believe that showing compassion and openness in order to understand and respect everyone’s pain is one way to move forward. That is what we are trying to do with this report. I am honoured to publish my first article with La Converse: a collection of reflections from five people who describe how that fateful day changed their lives or their view of the world.
Les entrevues de ce reportage ont été ra: The interviews for this report were gathered over a period of one month with the help of journalists Melissa Haouari, in Montréal, and Laviza Syed, in Toronto. In the interest of transparency, there are two things I want to share with you. First, we tried, without success, to include a voice from Lebanon. Over the course of a year, more than 2,000 people there have been killed and thousands more displaced as a result of Israeli cross-border attacks. Everyone we spoke to on the ground was too fearful and distrustful – of Western media and of Israeli surveillance tactics – to share their story with us.
Ensuite, toutes les entrevues avec nos s: Second, all of the interviews with our sources are presented in full, with the exception of the account of Raquel Look, a mother who lost her son on October 7. After consulting several trusted people from the Muslim and Jewish communities, Melissa, Laviza and I chose not to share the second part of the conversation, which brought to light Raquel Look’s anger toward Palestinians. By making this decision, we were able to stay true to the goal we set for ourselves in preparing this report: to widen hearts and minds by getting to know “the other.”
La douleur, rappelons-le, est universell: Pain, let us remember, is universal.
Le 7 octobre 2023, des hommes armés du H: On October 7, 2023, armed Hamas men crossed the border between Gaza and Israel, where they attacked military bases and killed Israeli civilians. As a result of the attack, nearly 1,205 people were killed, including 36 children. 251 people were taken hostage.
Le 8 octobre 2023, le cabinet de sécurit: On October 8, 2023, Israel’s security cabinet officially declared war on Hamas. The Israeli Defense Forces have killed more than 41,000 Palestinians, including more than 15,000 children. Thousands more Palestinians are believed to be trapped under the rubble, and almost the entire population of Gaza has been displaced. Since then, 117 Israeli hostages have been released.

‍<em>Yonatan Zeigen est un travailleur s: ‍Yonatan Zeigen is a social worker and mediator from Tel Aviv. His mother, Vivian Silver, 74, was killed on October 7. Today, Yonatan continues the peacebuilding work begun by his mother with the Parents Circle-Families Forum, a community-based organization in Beit Jala and Ramat Ef’al that brings together Palestinian and Israeli families who have lost members because of the conflict. Here he recalls the moments leading up to his mother’s death, as she hid in a closet at Kibbutz Be’eri.
« Au début [de l’attaque], on s’est parl: “At the beginning [of the attack], we talked and texted throughout the morning. We were rather calm and trying to pass the time. We kept joking around. Then, at some point, it became clear that the Israeli army wasn’t coming, and that Hamas wasn’t trying to take control of the kibbutz, but that it was a massacre. So we were able to say goodbye, knowing it was a farewell. In her last message, she wrote to me that Hamas was inside the house. What Hamas did on October 7 – and what Israel has been doing in Gaza ever since – is the result of a lifetime of conflict and a continuing occupation. And if we want a different reality, we have to behave differently – and not keep doing the same thing.”
« Ma mère était toujours très occupée. E: “My mother was always very busy. She worked a lot and devoted herself to many causes and initiatives. But as her son, I always felt like I was the most important thing in her life. That was the kind of woman she was.”
Vivian Silver était connue pour son mili: Vivian Silver was known for her peace activism and personally drove sick children from Gaza to the hospital, her friends said.
«Au début de la vingtaine, j’ai entrepri: “In my early twenties, I started law school to become a human rights lawyer. I dropped out when my first child was born. I gave up on the idea that I could have an impact on anything, and I became a social worker.”
«Mais depuis le 7 octobre, j’éprouve le: “But since October 7, I feel a need and a responsibility to get involved and use my voice to help bring about change. If my mother had survived, I can easily imagine her saying that revenge is not a solution and that peace is the only way to ensure Israel’s security. She would be very active in trying to stop the war and reach a comprehensive agreement.”
«Avant le 7 octobre, j’ai essayé de mene: “Before October 7, I tried to lead a normal life, working as a social worker and raising my children, but I always felt a certain sense of alienation, without knowing exactly what it was. Today, when I think about my work, I feel very close to what I do.”
« Je rencontre fréquemment des Palestini: “I meet with Palestinians frequently. It’s strange, because we have a very easy and natural relationship. It’s so simple, and you can’t achieve that in a collective context. If I’m able to sit down with a Palestinian who has also lost loved ones and we can build a relationship, everyone should be able to do it. It’s frustrating that we can’t do it as entire peoples, but it also proves that it’s possible, and that it’s very simple, right?”
« Je m’investis maintenant dans la seule: “I am now investing myself in the only thing that matters in Israel: Palestine. Nothing else matters if we don’t end the occupation and resolve the conflict. In that sense, I feel fulfilled to be able to do what I do. I wish I didn’t have to. I wish we lived in a context where it wouldn’t matter.”
Zeigen travaille désormais avec le Paren: Zeigen now works with the Parents Circle-Families Forum, based in Beit Jala and Ramat Ef’al, a grassroots organization of Palestinian and Israeli families who have lost immediate family members because of the conflict.
<em>Hamza Banar, 18 ans, est étudiant en: Hamza Banar, 18, is a first-year student in design and multimedia publishing at Al-Azhar University in Egypt. He and his family were displaced; they originally lived in the Shujaiya neighbourhood in central Gaza.
Hamza Banar fréquentait l’Université Al-: Hamza Banar attended Al-Azhar University in Gaza.
« Après le 7 octobre, la guerre a commen: “After October 7, the war started and destroyed everything. It destroyed my education, my future, my university and the house we lived in. We were displaced from the north to the south. We arrived in Deir el-Balah [a camp on the Gaza coast] after several forced displacements. We are exhausted. We have become responsible for everything, like going long distances to get water and food, and going to the market to communicate with the outside world.”
« Notre tente est un petit espace de qua: “Our tent is a small space of four metres by four metres, made up of a kitchen, a bathroom, a sleeping area and a living area for the eight members of my family. Food and water are hard to get, because they are increasingly scarce.”
« Les bombardements ont continué, mais o: “The bombing continued, but we tried to adapt. We couldn’t even finish our first week at the Tel Al-Hawa school we were attending. Shortly afterward, we were told to leave Gaza City immediately and head south, which was considered a safe humanitarian zone. We moved to the town of Al-Nusairat and went to take shelter at the Khaled Bin Al-Walid school, but we still weren’t safe. Several days went by. The intensity of the bombing on the school and the smoke coming from it kept us from sleeping. On December 27, artillery was used against the school, which forced us to evacuate the area once again.”
« Nous avons fui la ville à pied, y lais: “We fled the city on foot, leaving all our belongings behind, with no specific destination. We finally stayed with a relative for two days, then we set up our tent in Deir el-Balah, where we are living now.
Je suis très triste de ce qui est arrivé: I am very sad about what happened to our home. The memories we had there with my family, my relatives and my neighbours were wonderful. We dream of going back one day.”

<em>Raquel Look est une Montréalaise de: Raquel Look is a Jewish Montrealer. On October 7, her son, Alexandre, loses his life at the Supernova festival in the Negev desert in southern Israel. She now describes how that date radically changed her view of the world.
« Le 7 octobre, j’ai reçu un appel de mo: “On October 7, I got a call from my son, who was on vacation in Israel. He had gone there to take part in the music festival. In the early morning, he called me to say they had been attacked by rockets and were heading to a shelter.”
« Avant le 7 octobre, je me rendais souv: “Before October 7, I often travelled to Israel with my whole family. Missile fire and terrorist threats were commonplace. ‘Aren’t you used to it?’ I said to him on the phone. ‘No, but this time it’s really intense,’ he had replied.”
Le fils de Raquel, Alexandre, a été tué: Raquel’s son, Alexandre, was killed by Hamas militants on October 7.
«L’appel a duré près d’une heure et demi: “The call lasted nearly an hour and a half. At one point, Hamas terrorists arrived and there was a lot of commotion. It was panic. I still remember Alexandre trying to negotiate with the terrorists, who were arriving armed to the teeth, with the few words of Arabic he knew, in vain, sadly. Alexandre was killed by those who had come to terrorize the young festivalgoers. When rescuers arrived at the shelter where my son had lost his life, they found him with his arms open in an embrace, as if he were still protecting someone.”
« Aujourd’hui, j’ai peur. Lorsque je mar: “Today, I am afraid. When I walk through the streets of my city and see hundreds of people demonstrating in keffiyehs that show only their eyes, I think of those who cowardly took my son’s life. For me, October 7 is a date that must never be forgotten. It was a violent assault on the lives of people who only wanted to have fun, leaving behind a grieving mother. The mayor of the borough of Côte-Saint-Luc agreed to dedicate a square to the memory of my son.”
<em>Mohammed R. Mhawish est un journalis: Mohammed R. Mhawish is a Palestinian journalist originally from Gaza City. Following the Israeli bombing, he took refuge in Cairo in May with his wife and two children. In December, the Mhawish family survived the bombing of their home.
Le journaliste palestinien Mohammed R Mh: Palestinian journalist Mohammed R Mhawish was trapped under the rubble of his home for hours after an Israeli Defense Forces attack last December.
« Le 7 octobre, la vie de ma famille a c: “On October 7, my family’s life changed forever. In a matter of seconds, all I felt was that I was trapped under what turned out to be the ceiling of my home, which had come down on my family. When I regained consciousness, the first thing I remember is hearing voices. Even then, all I cared about was my family and making sure they were safe. Blood was spurting from my arms and my crushed fingers.”
« Les gens m’ont raconté ce qui s’est en: “People told me what happened next. My whole family had been injured, but what I remember most is my son, screaming, his face covered in blood and dust, while strangers tried to clean him up.”
« Les soins médicaux sont difficiles à o: “Medical care is hard to get, with hospitals crippled by the bombing and the lack of supplies, which leads to infections and deaths. Moving around in the north of the Gaza Strip, you risk being shot at or caught in crossfire. Yet hundreds of thousands of people have stayed put despite the Israeli order to leave. Infections are a constant fear, and we had to clean our wounds with boiling water. A week went by, and our health improved, but the bombing continued. On December 14, our neighbourhood was hit by an intense airstrike. The wounded were left where they lay, because stopping to help them would have meant certain death.”
«Au cours de l’année écoulée, je n’ai ja: “Over the past year, I have never managed to detach myself from what was happening. I am still part of the reality on the ground in Gaza, whether as a journalist or as a resident. On a personal level, I still have loved ones there. There are still family members, friends, people who are very dear to me, and they are still suffering famine, bombing and forced displacement.
« Mon aîné, Rafiq, qui a maintenant troi: “My eldest, Rafiq, who is now three, spent entire nights crying from hunger and cold in Gaza. He suffered from malnutrition. As Palestinians, we have no choice but to be resilient. We are forced [to be resilient] because it is part of our daily reality. We have to deal with what is happening. Every day, you wake up to the worst version of the same challenges, but you have to find a new way to live, to navigate between life and death, to survive the bombs, all while joking with your children so they don’t fall asleep frightened or terrorized.”
<em>Yipeng Ge est médecin généraliste et: Yipeng Ge is a general practitioner and public health specialist. He was previously a resident physician at the University of Ottawa’s Faculty of Medicine. Last November, the university suspended him for posting pro-Palestinian messages on social media. In February, he travelled to Gaza with a team of doctors from the humanitarian organizations Humanity Auxilium and Glia.
Le Dr Yipeng Ge s'est rendu à Gaza avec: Dr. Yipeng Ge has travelled to Gaza with a medical team since October 7. Photo: Alex Fizzard
« Lorsqu’ils m’ont suspendu, je travaill: “When they suspended me, I was still working with my patients; a lot of people don’t know that and don’t acknowledge it. The director of my clinic at the time reached out to me and offered his support. At the same time, I was very frustrated by the way these institutions treated me. In the end, they didn’t understand what public health is; they were unaware that I have training in the colonial determinants of health and that I approach the question of Palestine from the standpoint of settler colonialism and Zionist settler colonialism. That’s what I did during my master’s in public health, in the Palestine program of Harvard University’s Department of Health and Human Rights. If only someone had reached out and said: ‘We saw these posts on social media and we have questions. Can we have a conversation about it?’ Instead, they decided not to engage in discussion, to suspend me and to tell me: ‘You are a danger to yourself and to others’ – which is a flagrant case of anti-Palestinian racism, right?”
« Je n’aurais jamais pensé que les gens: “I never thought people could go so far to attack and destroy a person’s character and integrity. Having different opinions is one thing, and we can talk about it… but people didn’t even want to talk about it. That’s pretty ironic in academia, isn’t it? I was born in China. I came to Canada at the age of four; I grew up in Waterloo, Ontario. I had a lot of opportunities and privileges growing up there. The city is located near the territory of the Six Nations of the Grand River, the largest First Nations reserve in Canada. It doesn’t have drinking water. That really struck me: what is my role as a Canadian citizen? Who has benefited from these stolen lands, from the genocide of Indigenous peoples, from settler colonialism in the Canadian context? Now that I know all this, what should I do? It was a turning point. I chose to look into the question, and it’s what has driven me ever since.”
« Mes parents me soutiennent beaucoup. E: “My parents are very supportive. They have also learned a lot, which helped them understand what I had been doing all these years and helped them piece things together. They went to the student encampment and to the protests for Palestine. My father now brings back watermelon pins from China, where he works, and I hand them out to people. One day, my keffiyeh started to fray, and my mother said to me: ‘I can fix it for you.’
Les gens disent que Gaza et la Palestine: People say that Gaza and Palestine teach us about life, and that’s completely true. It is ironic that Palestinians are experiencing a genocidal campaign that is trying to erase them, their community and their people from the face of the Earth. In the face of that, they show so much life and humanity, and they choose love and compassion. The first night, when I arrived in Gaza, the local people immediately brought us food and water. I sobbed uncontrollably for a quarter of an hour. I said to myself: ‘My God, what am I doing? These people have lived through hell, and I don’t want them to have to support me in my grief and my emotions.’”
